passages.title: Oath by Mecca: humankind created for struggle
passages.tafsir:
Sūrah al-Balad opens with a single sworn statement that runs across four verses. Allah swears by the sacred city of Makkah, and by the begetter and what he begot — and between the two, He addresses His Prophet ﷺ concerning that same city. Then comes the thing all of it was sworn to establish: the human being was made for toil. The first three verses are the oath; the fourth is what the oath is about, and every word before it leans toward it.

## The "no" that opens an oath

The passage begins with a small word that puzzles many readers: *lā uqsimu* — literally "I do not swear," yet rendered "I do swear by this city."

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** notes that one view is that this particle *lā* ("no") carries no independent meaning here, and that such particles are commonplace in Arabic. But it judges the more appropriate view to be this: when a sūrah opens with *lā* followed by an oath, it was revealed to refute a false assumption held by the opponents. The sense becomes: *No — what you disbelievers are saying and thinking is not correct; the truth is what We are about to swear to.*

**Ibn Kathir** records the same reading from Mujahid (transmitted by Khusayf), who said the word *Lā* refers to the refutation against the Quraysh — "I swear by this city."

So the sūrah does not merely begin; it begins by pushing something aside. Before Allah tells man what he is, He clears away what man imagines himself to be. And what He clears it away with is an oath by a place and by a people.

## What is sworn by: a dwelling, and its dwellers

Ibn Kathir gives the architecture of the oath in one stroke, and it is worth holding on to as we read: Allah swears by the Mother of the Towns, which are **dwellings** — and then He swears by the **dwellers** therein. Place first, then people. Once you see that, the three verses stop being three separate remarks and become one gesture.

**The city.** Ibn ʿAbbās, in a report from ʿIkrimah transmitted by Shabīb bin Bishr, said simply that *this city* means Makkah; Ibn Kathir describes it as the Mother of the Towns. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to the parallel oath in Sūrah at-Tīn (95:3), where Allah swears "by this peaceful City" — the adjective attached to the City there is *peaceful* — and says this shows the superiority and honour of Makkah over other cities.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then places beside this a report from Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh Ibn ʿAdiyy: when the Prophet ﷺ was migrating from Makkah to Madinah, he addressed the city itself and said, "By Allah, you are dearer to Allah than the entire earth. If I was not forced out of this place, I would never have abandoned you." (Transmitted by Tirmidhi and Ibn Mājah, cited via Mazhari.)

Hold that scene next to the oath. Allah swears by a city whose worth is beyond every other patch of earth — and the man who loved it most was driven out of it.

**The word spoken to the Prophet ﷺ about that city.** This is the most discussed phrase in the passage, and the classical commentators read it in more than one way. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the possibilities and notes that Mazhari cites three and says all three are equally possible. Nothing here is settled; these are live alternatives among the scholars.

*First*, *ḥillun* may derive from *ḥulūl*, meaning to reside in or descend upon a place. On this reading it means "a dweller, a resident": the city of Makkah is sacred in itself, and since the Prophet ﷺ is an inhabitant of it, its sanctity, honour and glory are enhanced and augmented.

*Second*, *ḥillun* may derive from *ḥillatun*, "that whose doing is lawful" — and this yields two further senses. One is a bitter indictment of the Prophet's ﷺ persecutors: the pagans of Makkah consider it lawful to do him any harm, even to kill him, in this very city — a place so sacred that harming a living creature within its precincts, let alone killing or hunting it, is strictly forbidden *even according to their own belief system*. They will not disturb a living thing in the Ḥaram, yet they treat the blood of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as permissible there. The translation "even though you are subject to abuse in this city" carries this sense.

*Third*, it may be a prophecy: that Makkah would be made lawful for the Prophet ﷺ in the sense that fighting there would be allowed to him for a specified time, and that he would alight in the city — as happened at the Conquest of Makkah, when the injunctions and ordinances of the Ḥaram were suspended for one day.

Ibn Kathir reports this third sense from the early authorities. Ibn ʿAbbās explained the verse: "O Muhammad! It is permissible for you to fight in it." Similar is reported from Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Abū Ṣāliḥ, ʿAṭiyyah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatādah, as-Suddī and Ibn Zayd. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said that Allah made fighting in it lawful for him for one hour of a day.

Ibn Kathir supports this with a hadith he describes as agreed upon as authentic, in which the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah made this city sacred on the Day He created the heavens and the earth, so it is sacred by the sanctity of Allah until the Day of Judgement; its trees are not to be uprooted and its bushes and grasses not removed; it was made lawful for him only for one hour of a day; and today its sanctity has been restored just as it was sacred yesterday — "so let the one who is present inform those who are absent." In another wording, he added that if anyone tries to use the Messenger's fighting in Makkah as an excuse to fight there, tell him that Allah permitted it for His Messenger "and He has not permitted it for you."

Notice what that does. Whatever exception was granted is sealed shut the moment anyone reaches for it. The permission was personal, for one hour, and the sanctity closed over the city again like water.

**The dwellers.** The oath now names the people. Ibn Kathir reports that Mujāhid, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Qatādah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Sufyān ath-Thawrī, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, as-Suddī, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Khuṣayf, Shuraḥbīl bin Saʿd and others held that *the begetter* is Ādam, the father of mankind, and *what he begot* is his children. Ibn Kathir calls this view "good and strong," and supports it precisely by the dwelling-then-dweller logic above. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the same position, adding that *what he begot* covers his children from the inception of the world to its end.

Two other views are recorded, and the sources present them as genuine differences rather than as one settled answer. Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī said it refers to Ibrāhīm and his progeny; Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim both record this. Ibn Jarīr himself preferred that the phrase is general — every father and every child he fathers — and Ibn Kathir says this meaning is also acceptable. (The rendering "and by every parent and their child" follows this general reading.)

Either way, by the time the fourth verse arrives Allah has sworn by the holiest ground on earth and by every human being who has ever stood on it. The oath has gathered up the whole species — and now it tells that entire lineage what it was made for.

## The thing sworn to: created *fī kabad*

**"Indeed, We have created humankind in constant struggle."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *kabad* means labour, toil or difficulty: the verse says that man's life is a series of hard and toilsome works. It is not that hardship happens to us; it is the medium we were created inside of — the Arabic says created *fī* kabad, *in* it.

The early commentators fill this in with startling concreteness rather than abstraction:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās** (reported by Ibn Abī Najīḥ and Jurayj from ʿAṭāʾ) said, "He was created while in hardship. Don't you see him?" — and then mentioned his birth, and the sprouting of his teeth.
- **Mujāhid** said: "A drop of sperm, then a clot, then a lump of flesh, enduring in his creation," and cited Allah's words, "His mother bears him with hardship. And she brings him forth with hardship" (46:15) — adding that she breast-feeds him with hardship, and his livelihood is a hardship, and he endures all of this.
- **Saʿīd bin Jubayr**: "In hardship and seeking livelihood."
- **ʿIkrimah**: "In hardship and long-suffering."
- **Qatādah**: "In difficulty."
- **Al-Ḥasan**: "Enduring the hardships of the world by life and the severity of the Hereafter."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a fuller version of Ibn ʿAbbās's list, and it is worth reading slowly, because it is the shape of a whole life: conception and confinement in the mother's womb; the mother's pangs of birth; the hardship of sucking the mother's milk and the difficulty of weaning; then the pursuit of livelihood and the other necessities of life; then the hardships and long-suffering of old age, death, the grave, resurrection, the accounting of one's deeds before Allah, and reward and punishment.

Notice that the list does not stop at the graveside. Al-Ḥasan's comment and Ibn ʿAbbās's both push *kabad* past death and into the Hereafter. The struggle a person is created in is not finished by dying.

## Why the human being in particular

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious objection and answers it: these difficulties are not confined to man — other animals share them too. Man is singled out because of his intelligence. The more the power of a creature's intelligence, the higher the degree of legal obligation upon it. And the greatest difficulty of all is borne at resurrection and the life after death, when we will be required to give an account of the deeds we did throughout our lives — something other species will not be required to do.

It further reports that some scholars say no creation suffers as much difficulty as human beings, despite the human body being smaller and weaker than most other animals; what is most powerful is man's brainpower, and so he has been specifically mentioned here.

## The oath turned into evidence

Here the whole structure pays off. Citing Qurṭubī, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reasons: by swearing an oath by Makkah, by Ādam and by his children, Allah has made plain that man was created in difficulties and to endure hardships — and this is itself a proof that man did not come into existence on his own. His Creator is an All-Powerful Being who, in His wisdom, created every species of creation with its own specific predisposition and capacity for action. **Had man had any part in his own creation, he would never have allowed such difficulties and hardships for himself.** The very thing we complain about is the fingerprint of a Maker other than ourselves.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the practical conclusion directly from the oath and its subject: a person's desire to live peacefully and comfortably in this world without enduring any hardship is a silly idea and a false notion — it is simply not going to happen. Difficulty, hardship, distress and affliction are bound to befall every person.

And since they are bound to come anyway, the wise response is not to spend a life trying to negotiate them away. It is, in the words of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, to be in readiness to work hard for something that may help in an eternal life — and the only factor that will help there is faith and obedience to the Truth.

This is the quiet mercy inside a severe verse. If you were made for struggle, then struggle is not a sign that something has gone wrong with your life; it is the condition you were designed for. Allah swore by the most honoured place on earth, and by every parent and child who ever walked it, to tell you so. The only question left is what you spend that struggle on.

passages.title: The arrogant man's boast of squandered wealth
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah al-Balad 90:5–7

**The passage in brief.** Three short verses draw the portrait of a particular kind of man. Ayah 5 exposes an assumption he carries silently — that nobody has any power over him. Ayah 6 lets us hear him speak, and what comes out is a boast about the fortune he has poured out. Ayah 7 exposes the second assumption — that nobody sees him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that ayah 7 comes "after describing a few of the ignorant disbeliever's qualities," and speaks "about an unbeliever." The three verses move as one accusation: *no one can touch me → look how much I have spent → and no one is even watching.*

Ibn Kathir heads this whole section with a phrase worth holding on to: **"Man is encompassed by Allah and His Bounties."**

## Ayah 5: "Do they think that no one has power over them?"

**أَيَحۡسَبُ أَن لَّن يَقۡدِرَ عَلَيۡهِ أَحَدٌ** — *"Do they think that no one has power over them,"* which Ibn Kathir renders, *"Does he think that none can overcome him?"*

Notice the form of the verse. It does not say "he says"; it says **"does he think."** This is not a claim the man makes out loud — that comes in the next verse. This is what he assumes underneath the boast.

The early scholars read the phrase in two complementary ways:

- **Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī**: "Meaning no one is able to take his wealth." This is the man's felt sense of security. His money is his fortress; nothing and no one can reach in and remove it.
- **Qatādah**: "The Son of Adam thinks that he will not be asked about this wealth of his — how he earned and how he spent it." This is the deeper delusion: not merely that his wealth is safe, but that he will never stand and answer for it.

Between the two readings you get the whole disease. He thinks nothing can be *taken* from him, and he thinks nothing will be *asked* of him. Qatādah's gloss repays sitting with, because he names precisely the two questions this man never expects to face: **how he earned it and how he spent it.**

## Ayah 6: the boast — "I have wasted enormous wealth!"

**يَقُولُ أَهۡلَكۡتُ مَالٗا لُّبَدًا** — *boasting, "I have wasted enormous wealth!"* Ibn Kathir renders it, *"He says: 'I have wasted wealth in abundance!'"* and explains: "This means, the Son of Adam says, 'I spent an abundance of wealth.'" This is the reading of **Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, as-Suddī and others**.

Feel the gap between what the man **means** and what he has actually admitted. In his own mouth this is a brag: *I spent a fortune.* He wants to be admired for the sheer scale of what passed through his hands — the quantity is the whole point of the sentence for him. But the verse presents it as *wasting*, not as achievement. He thinks he is listing his triumphs; he is in fact reading out an inventory of loss.

And notice where this verse sits. It stands between two questions — about being **overpowered** and about being **seen** — because the boast is the evidence for both charges. A man who expected to be asked how he earned and how he spent his wealth, as Qatādah put it, could not turn his spending into a party piece. The bragging is the symptom; the two false assumptions are the illness.

## Ayah 7: "Do they think that no one sees them?"

**أَيَحۡسَبُ أَن لَّمۡ يَرَهُۥٓ أَحَدٌ** — *"Do they think that no one sees them?"*; Ibn Kathir: *"Does he think that none sees him?"*

The question of ayah 5 returns in the same shape. *Does he think that none can overcome him?* … *Does he think that none sees him?* Twice the same question, twice the same "no one." Only the middle changes: first **power**, then **sight**. The repetition is itself the argument. He has built his life on two "no ones," and neither one exists.

**Mujāhid** states the meaning plainly: "Does he think that **Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, does not see him**." Ibn Kathir adds that "others among the Salaf have said similar to this."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān specifies what it is that is being seen — "that is, **his evil deeds**" — and then gives the conclusion in a single sentence: "He should realise that his Creator watches every action of his."

That is the answer to the whole passage. Not an argument, not a threat — simply the fact he had overlooked. He is seen. The earning is seen and the spending is seen; the display is seen and what stands behind it is seen. And the One who sees is the One he imagined had no power over him.

## Living it

**Expect the reckoning on both sides of the ledger.** Qatādah's gloss is the practical heart of this passage: the question is not only *how much*, but **how you earned it and how you spent it**. Two separate questions. A clean income spent on vanity fails the second; a lavish charity out of a filthy source fails the first.

**Watch what your boasting reveals.** The man of ayah 6 is not condemned for having wealth, but for the pleasure he takes in announcing how much of it he has burned through. Whenever we catch ourselves narrating our spending for effect, ayah 5 is asking what we quietly assume about accountability.

**Never mistake untouchable for unaccountable.** Al-Ḥasan's reading — "no one is able to take his wealth" — describes a real feeling that money produces. But security in the world is not the same thing as safety before Allah.

**Live as one who is seen.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reduces the passage to a sentence worth carrying through an ordinary day: "He should realise that his Creator watches every action of his." The man in these three verses spent his life's effort on a boast, because he thought the room was empty. It never was.
</tafsir>

passages.title: Allah's gifts: eyes, tongue, and two paths
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

*"Have We not given them two eyes, a tongue, and two lips; and shown them the two ways ˹of right and wrong˺?"*

Three short ayat, one continuous argument. Maarif ul Quran sets the scene: the preceding ayah "pointed out the ignorance and heedlessness of man. He thinks that Allah has no power over him, and that there is no one watching over his actions." These ayat are the answer, and they are framed not as a lecture but as a question the man cannot answer with "no" — *Did We not make for him…?* Allah does not send him off to survey the heavens for proof. He points him at his own face. As Maarif ul Quran puts it, "the current verse mentions a few of the organs and abilities that Allah has endowed him with. If he reflects carefully on these endowments, he will appreciate His infinite wisdom and power **within himself**."

Four gifts are named — two eyes, a tongue, two lips, and the showing of the two roads — and the commentaries treat them as one inventory rather than four separate topics. The equipment for seeing, the equipment for speaking, and the capacity to tell right from wrong all arrive together, from one Giver, and all point the same way.

## The evidence he is carrying: eyes, a tongue, two lips

Ibn Kathir's gloss on the first two gifts is deliberately plain, and each phrase names a purpose:

- *"Have We not made for him two eyes?"* — **"meaning, for him to see with them."**
- *"And a tongue"* — **"meaning, for him to speak with, and so that he can express that which is inside of him."**
- *"and two lips?"* — **"In order to help him with speaking, eating food, and beautifying his face and his mouth."**

Maarif ul Quran lingers where Ibn Kathir moves on, and it is worth slowing down with it, because this is a passage that asks you to *look* at the thing you look with. It describes the optic nerves and tissues as "rather delicate," sending nervous impulses to the brain when stimulated by light rays from external objects. It describes each eye as a hollow, spherical capsule made up of several layers and structures, set into a socket in the skull. And then it notes how thoroughly that fragile instrument is *defended*:

- the eyelids, which close on their own when a harmful object is seen coming from the front — "it works like an automatic machine"
- the eyelashes, which block the dust from getting into the eyes
- the eyebrows, which help keep things from falling into the eyes directly from the top
- the facial bones — the orbit and the cheek bones — which protect the eye if one were to fall on one's face, or if something were to fall on the face

Then, in the same breath, the commentary turns to the second gift. It calls the tongue "the most amazing and important creation" — "the long piece of flesh fixed to the bottom of the mouth that can represent thoughts of the heart." That is the same point Ibn Kathir makes in his own words: the tongue is given *so that he can express that which is inside of him*. Both commentaries treat it not as a mere muscle but as the organ by which what is hidden becomes audible.

Maarif ul Quran traces the chain: a thought occurs in the heart, the brain interprets it and prepares the appropriate topic and words, and the tongue utters them — the whole task performed so swiftly "that the listener does not even realise how many systems have worked before the distinguishable sounds, letters and words were uttered." The two lips, it notes, play an important role in articulating those different sounds, letters and words.

**Then comes the warning that gives these gifts their weight.** Maarif ul Quran observes that this swift-working articulator may, within half a minute, utter a word that takes a man out from Hell and admits him into Paradise — the word of faith — or that endears him to his enemy in this world, as by seeking forgiveness of his shortcomings. And the same tongue, within the same short span of time, may take him to Hell by uttering the word of disbelief, or may turn his closest friend into his biggest enemy by using obscene language against him. "The tongue has many benefits as well as many ways of destruction. It is a double-edged sword that can operate against an enemy, and it can also cut one's own throat."

And here the commentary offers a beautiful reading of why the lips are mentioned at all in an ayah about speech: *"Therefore, Allah has kept it covered within the case of two lips. Probably, this is the reason why the pair of lips is mentioned. The Creator Who has endowed man with tongue has equipped him with a pair of lips in order to protect it."* The lips are the sheath. And so the practical conclusion is drawn directly from the anatomy: **"Therefore, he should be careful in its use. He should not unsheathe it unnecessarily."**

## The gift that completes the list: two roads he cannot miss

The inventory does not stop at organs. Maarif ul Quran continues the same sentence into the fourth gift: Allah "has equipped him with a pair of eyes, a pair of lips and a tongue, and has equipped him with the ability to distinguish good from evil and right from wrong." Ibn Kathir gives this ayah its own heading, and the heading is the point: **the ability to distinguish between good and evil is also a blessing.** Moral clarity is not a burden laid on top of the gifts; it is on the same list as eyesight.

**The word.** Maarif ul Quran explains that *najdain* (النَّجْدَيْن) is "the dual form of *najd* which means an elevated or conspicuous road," and that the word "signifies the two high and conspicuous ways of good and evil, or of success and destruction." These are not hidden trails needing a guide with secret knowledge. They stand out.

**What the two ways are.** Ibn Kathir says simply, "This refers to the two paths," and then reports — through Sufyan Ath-Thawri from 'Asim, from Zirr — that 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud said of *"And shown him the two ways?"*: **"The good and the evil."** He notes that similar has been reported from 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Abu Wa'il, Abu Salih, Muhammad bin Ka'b, Ad-Dahhak, and 'Ata' Al-Khurasani, among others — a long line of the earliest interpreters converging on the same short answer.

**The Qur'an's own parallel.** Ibn Kathir places alongside it Allah's words: *"Verily, We have created man from Nutfah Amshaj, in order to try him: so We made him hearer and seer. Verily, We showed him the way, whether he be grateful or ungrateful"* (76:2–3). The shape of that ayah matches ours exactly — the senses are given, the way is shown, and the whole of it is a **test**.

**Two layers of guidance.** Maarif ul Quran connects this ayah to Allah's words *"then inspired it with its [instinct of] evil and piety"* (91:8) and draws the conclusion: **"Thus in the first instance man receives guidance from his own conscience. This is supported by the guidance of the Holy Prophets (ʿalayhim as-salām — peace be upon them) and celestial books that clarify it."** An inner witness, and then an outer confirmation sent down to clarify it. Both are gifts.

**And the choice is real.** He has been shown the two ways "so that he may choose between the two. Obviously, he should choose the good way. **In his make-up, there exists the ability to take either way.**"

## Three ayat, one case

Maarif ul Quran states the verdict the whole passage has been building toward: the ignorant and heedless person "who denies the power of the Omnipotent, should look into his own being, he would be able to observe **His attribute of perfect power and consummate wisdom**." And then the line that binds the three ayat into one sentence — **"He should observe with his two eyes and confess with his tongue."**

Follow the order of that sentence and the three ayat fall into place: he is to observe with the eyes of ayah 8, confess with the tongue of ayah 9, and then choose between the two ways of ayah 10 — for, as the commentary goes on immediately to say, he was shown them "so that he may choose between the two."

## Living it

**Your eyes were issued to you with a purpose.** Ibn Kathir says they were given "for him to see with them." Maarif ul Quran says what he ought to have seen: perfect power and consummate wisdom, observable in his own being. Sight that never once turns on the endowments the commentary asks him to reflect upon is sight used against its design.

**Your tongue is sheathed for a reason.** If it is a double-edged sword, the question is not only *is what I am about to say true?* but the one Maarif ul Quran actually presses: does this need to be unsheathed at all? "He should be careful in its use. He should not unsheathe it unnecessarily." And take heart from the other edge — the same half minute that can turn a closest friend into an enemy can also carry the word of faith, or the seeking of forgiveness that endears a man even to his enemy.

**The roads are conspicuous; the choosing is yours.** *Najdain* means elevated and clearly visible ways. Between the guidance of one's own conscience and the guidance of the Prophets and the revealed books that clarify it, the signposts are not hidden. What is left is the choice — and, as the commentary says plainly, "obviously, he should choose the good way," for "in his make-up, there exists the ability to take either way."

The man the surah describes was not short of equipment. He had two eyes to see with, a tongue to say what he saw, two lips to guard it, and two clearly marked roads in front of him — and he had convinced himself that no one was watching.

passages.title: The steep ascent: freeing captives, feeding the hungry
passages.tafsir:
> # The Steep Ascent (90:11–16)

These six ayat name the climb that most people never begin. Allah points to a steep pass and says that man has not taken it. Then, in a rare move, He tells us exactly what that pass is made of: an unfastened neck, a meal on a day of hunger, an orphan of one's own family, a destitute man in the dust. What holds the passage together is that single image of ascent, and the fact that Allah Himself defines it — not with slogans, but with acts you can count.

## The word that carries the passage: ʿaqabah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word carefully. *ʿAqabah* means "hill, high place or a steep road." It can also mean the opposite — "a low area of land between two hills or mountains, that is, a valley."

Why would one word hold both a summit and a valley? Because of what an *ʿaqabah* does for a person. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, an *ʿaqabah* "helps a man in saving himself when pursued by an enemy by ascending the summit of the mountain, or in escaping by descending into the valley." It is the hard terrain that is also the escape route. You do not take it because it is pleasant. You take it because it is the way out.

So the word is chosen for its function, not just its shape. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion directly: "Here the word ʿaqabah refers to obedience and devotion. Just as it saves man from an enemy, righteous deeds save man from the punishment of the Hereafter."

That reframes everything that follows. Ayat 13–16 are not a list of nice things to do. They are the pass through the mountain, taken while something is behind you.

## Ayah 11: a verdict, and underneath it, a summons

Ibn Kathir renders ayah 11: "But he has not attempted to pass on the path that is steep." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: "Yet he did not make his way through the steep course." The verb (*iqtaḥama*) is not the verb of a stroll — every rendering reaches for effort: *attempted to pass, made his way through*.

Ibn Kathir then quotes the early commentator **Ibn Zayd**, who hears in the ayah not only a report but a challenge: "This means, will he not traverse upon the path which contains salvation and good?"

That double sense matters. Read one way, ayah 11 is an accusation: here is a man who has not started up the hill. Read Ibn Zayd's way, it is an open door — *why not climb it?* And notice what he says the pass contains: **salvation and good.** The road that looks like nothing but cost is the road out.

## Ayah 12: Allah asks, then Allah answers

"And what will make you know the path that is steep?"

The question is put to the listener, and the listener has no answer — which is the point. Left to ourselves, we would fill in "the steep path" with something grand and rare. Ibn Kathir preserves Ibn Zayd's observation that Allah does not leave it to guesswork: "Then He explains this path by his saying, *And what will make you know the path that is steep? Freeing a neck, or giving food.*"

Everything from ayah 13 onward is Allah's own definition of the ascent.

## Ayah 13: unfastening a neck

*Fakku raqabah* — Ibn Kathir renders it "Freeing a neck"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, "freeing of the neck of a slave." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it "a great devotional act," and gives the reason in one phrase: **"it moulds a man's life."** It does not merely relieve a person; it remakes the shape of his existence.

Ibn Kathir supports this ayah with several narrations. Imam Ahmad recorded, from Saʿīd bin Marjānah, that he heard Abū Hurayrah say that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Whoever frees a believing slave, Allah will free for every limb (of the slave) one of his limbs from the Fire. This is to such an extent that He (Allah) will free a hand for a hand, a leg for a leg, and a private part for a private part."

Al-Bukhārī, Muslim, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʾī all recorded this hadith from Saʿīd bin Marjānah.

Look at the exchange the Prophet ﷺ describes: the ayah speaks of a *neck*, and the reward is counted out limb by limb. You unfasten a body from bondage in this world; Allah unfastens your body from the Fire, part for part. The recompense is measured in the same currency as the deed.

And Ibn Kathir does not leave it as doctrine. In the very same report, **ʿAli bin al-Husayn** — hearing this — turned to Saʿīd and asked, "Did you hear this from Abū Hurayrah?" Saʿīd replied, "Yes." Then ʿAli bin al-Husayn said to a slave boy he owned, the swiftest of his servants, "Call Mutarrif!" And when the slave was brought before him, he said: **"Go, for you are free for the Face of Allah."**

He asked one question — *did you hear this yourself?* — and having been told yes, he acted. The report does not linger on his deliberation, because there is none to record.

Ibn Kathir adds a second narration. Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿAmr bin ʿAbasah that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Whoever builds a Masjid so that Allah may be remembered in it, Allah will build a house for him in Paradise; and whoever frees a Muslim person, then it will be his ransom from Hell; and whoever grows grey in Islam, then it will be a light for him on the Day of Judgement."

Through another route, Imam Ahmad recorded from Abū Umāmah, from ʿAmr bin ʿAbasah, a longer version in which the Prophet ﷺ mentioned, among other deeds, that "whoever frees a believing slave, then Allah will free each of his limbs from the Fire for every limb that the slave has." Ibn Kathir notes that Ahmad recorded this hadith "from different routes of transmission that are good and strong, and all praise is due to Allah."

Hold the two images together: a *ransom from Hell*, and a limb freed for a limb. Wealth spent to unfasten a neck comes back as one's own release.

## Ayah 14: food on a day of hunger

"Or giving food in a day full of *masghabah*." Ibn Kathir reports **Ibn ʿAbbās**: it means "of hunger" — and ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, ad-Dahhāk, Qatādah and others said the same. Ibn Kathir gives the root plainly: "The word *Saghb* means hunger."

The ayah does not say "feed the hungry." It says feed *on a day of hunger* — a day when hunger is in the air, when food is scarce and therefore precious and therefore hard to give away. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out exactly this: "feeding him in a day when he is hungry will attract more reward."

This is the logic of the whole passage. A steep road is steep. The deed is placed at the moment it costs you most.

## Ayat 15–16: the two people Allah names

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets up these two ayat as a refinement: "Although it is an act of great reward to feed any hungry person, it carries even a greater reward to feed certain people."

**"To an orphan near of kin" (ayah 15).** Ibn Kathir explains: "he gives food on a day like this to an orphan" who is *dhā maqrabah* — "meaning, who is related to him," as reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, al-Hasan, ad-Dahhāk and as-Suddī.

Why the relative? Because the deed doubles. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith collected by Imam Ahmad from Salmān bin ʿĀmir, who heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say:

> "Charity given to the poor person is counted as one charity, while if it is given to a relative it is counted as two: charity and connecting the ties (of kinship)."

At-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʾī both recorded this hadith, and Ibn Kathir states that its chain of narration is authentic. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same in its own words: the reward "is twofold, for satisfying the hunger of a hungry person and for maintaining family ties and fulfilling his rights."

There is a quiet weight in this. The orphan of your own family is the one whose need you are most likely to know about — and Allah names him first.

**"Or to a *miskīn* cleaving to dust" (ayah 16).** Ibn Kathir glosses *dhā matrabah*: "poor, miserable, and clinging to the dirt. It means those who are in a state of destitution." Then **Ibn ʿAbbās** gives the picture that no paraphrase improves: *dhā matrabah* is "that who is dejected in the street and who has no house or anything else to protect him against the dirt."

Not poor in the sense of struggling. Poor in the sense that there is nothing between him and the ground.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān completes the pairing: if the orphan "is not a close relative or family member, but he is so poor as to be wallowing in dust, spending on him will yield a greater reward." And then the principle behind both ayat: **"The poorer the person is, the greater will be the reward for the spender."**

So Allah gives two routes up the same pass — closeness of blood, or depth of need. Either one raises the deed.

## What makes this a climb at all

Read the four deeds together and a pattern appears. Each is placed at the point of greatest cost. The neck is unfastened by the one who owns it. The meal is given on the day of hunger, not on a day of plenty — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says plainly that this is where the reward increases. The orphan named is the one from your own family. The *miskīn* named is the one with nothing between him and the dirt — and again, "the poorer the person is, the greater will be the reward for the spender."

That is why it is an *ʿaqabah* and not a road. Nothing here is difficult to understand; all of it is difficult to do. And it is worth noticing where the difficulty sits: in every case, on what a person owns and would rather keep.

## Living it

The passage is unusually concrete, so the application can be too.

- **Direct your giving at the hardest, not the easiest, moment.** Ayah 14 rewards the meal given on the day of hunger. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: feeding him "in a day when he is hungry will attract more reward."
- **Start with your own relatives in need.** On the authority of Salmān bin ʿĀmir, giving to a relative counts twice: charity, and the joining of kinship. Ayah 15 makes the orphan of the family the named case.
- **Do not skip the man with nothing.** Ibn ʿAbbās's *dhā matrabah* — no house, nothing between him and the dirt — is written into the Qur'an so that he cannot be edited out of our charity.
- **Act on what you learn.** ʿAli bin al-Husayn confirmed the hadith with the man who had heard it, and then freed a slave of his own "for the Face of Allah." Knowledge of the reward was, for him, a thing to be spent rather than stored.

## Where the passage leaves us

Allah asked what the steep path is, and then answered His own question with four acts. That is the mercy inside the difficulty: no one has to guess at the route. Ibn Zayd read the ayah as an invitation — "will he not traverse upon the path which contains salvation and good?" — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names what the climb is for: as an *ʿaqabah* saves a man from an enemy, "righteous deeds save man from the punishment of the Hereafter."

The one who takes this pass is climbing away from something. And Allah has told him plainly where the road is.

passages.title: Belief, mutual counsel, and the people of the right
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

The ayat just before these listed the hard, costly deeds that make up "the path that is steep" — freeing a neck, giving food on a day of hunger, the orphan who is a relative, the destitute one clinging to the dust (ayat 11–16). Ayah 17 now adds faith to those deeds, and adds to faith something further: that a person urges others alongside him. Ayah 18 gives the verdict — such people are *aṣḥāb al-maymanah*, the people of the right.

The two ayat hold together as description and verdict: 17 describes the person, 18 declares where that person stands.

## "Then he became one of those who believed"

Ibn Kathir explains this clause simply and powerfully. It means, he says, "then, along with these beautiful and pure characteristics, he was a believer in his heart, seeking the reward of that from Allah."

Two things in that sentence deserve attention. First, *along with* — the faith is not a substitute for the freeing and the feeding, and the freeing and the feeding are not a substitute for it. Second, *in his heart, seeking the reward of that from Allah*. The deeds of ayat 13–16 are visible to everyone; this is the invisible thing underneath them, and Ibn Kathir names it as the place where the reward is sought.

He supports this with two other ayat in which Allah attaches the same condition to accepted action:

> "And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it, with the necessary effort due for it while he is believer, then such are the ones whose striving shall be appreciated." (17:19)

> "Whoever works righteousness – whether male or female – while being a true believer..." (16:97)

In both places the striving is real and the work is genuine, and still the clause "while he is believer" stands there as the hinge.

**A note on the two renderings.** Our two commentaries render ayah 17 differently. Ibn Kathir reads it positively: "Then he became one of those who believed and recommended one another to patience, and recommended one another to compassion." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it carrying a negation forward: "then he did not join those who believe and advise each other to be patient and advise each other to be merciful." Both, in their comments, arrive at the same requirement: for Ibn Kathir the believer is the one who has these qualities *along with* his good deeds; for Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, "the doing only of good actions mentioned in the foregoing verse is not enough."

## Two counsels, and why they are mutual

The verb in both halves of the ayah is *tawāṣaw*. The renderings in front of us all reach for a reciprocal sense: they "recommended **one another**" to patience; they "advise **each other**" to be patient and merciful. This is not one person preaching down at another. It is a two-way traffic of encouragement inside a community.

That reciprocity is the burden of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's comment here, which it titles *Obligations of a Believer*:

> "The verse points out that the doing only of good actions mentioned in the foregoing verse is not enough for raising the all round stature of the Muslim community. Good ideals and right principles, combined with continuous and sustained adherence to the path of moral rectitude and teaching of virtues to others, are equally essential."

So the ayah, in this reading, stacks layers on top of the deeds already named: *do* the hard good, *believe* while doing it, and then *teach* it — because personal action alone, however good, does not raise "the all round stature of the Muslim community." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it as a duty: the ayah "draws the attention of a believer to his socio-moral obligation to the effect that he ought to teach his other Muslim brothers to be patient and to be merciful."

## Ṣabr: not a mood, but a discipline

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a definition of *ṣabr* worth memorising, because it is broader than the usual English "patience":

> "The word *sabr* signifies 'to withhold oneself from evil deeds and to act upon good deeds.'"

So *ṣabr* here has two arms. One holds a person back from evil deeds; the other moves him into good ones. On this definition it is not merely passive endurance of misfortune — it is the whole steady exertion of a life lived under command. Which suits the image the surah has been using: a *ʿaqabah*, a path that is steep.

Ibn Kathir sharpens the application in one particular direction. Commenting on the pair of counsels together, he says of the one described here that he was "from the believers who worked righteous deeds, and advised each other to be patient with the harms of the people, and to be merciful with them."

Read that closely. The patience being urged is patience *with the harms of the people*. And it sits immediately beside mercy *toward those same people*. Ibn Kathir does not let the two be separated.

## Marḥamah: mercy as a way of being with people

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines *marḥamah* as "to show mercy to one another or to empathise with others and abstain from hurting them" — and then makes a striking claim about it: "This embraces almost all the injunctions of the entire religion."

That is a large statement, but look at what the definition covers. Mercy in this sense has an active side (show mercy, feel with people) and a restraining side (abstain from hurting them). Between those two, an enormous share of a person's dealings with other human beings is accounted for.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir brings three narrations at this point. The first he introduces as "the noble Hadith," without naming a collection:

> "The merciful people will be treated with mercy by the Most Merciful (Allah). Be merciful to those who are on the earth and He Who is above the heavens will be merciful to you."

The second he introduces simply as another hadith of the Prophet ﷺ, again without naming a collection:

> "Allah will not be merciful with whoever is not merciful with the people."

Because our source does not name a collection for either of these, we pass on the teaching without attaching one to it. The teaching itself is exact and sobering: the mercy a person shows is tied to the mercy he receives.

The third, Ibn Kathir attributes to **Abu Dawud**, recorded from ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr, who narrated it from the Prophet ﷺ:

> "Whoever does not show mercy to our children, nor does he recognize the right of our elders, then he is not of us."

Mercy is named here at the two ends of a community — the young, and the old whose right is to be recognised.

## Ayah 18: "These are the people of the right"

Then comes the verdict, and Ibn Kathir's comment on it is as brief as the ayah itself. On *"They are those on the Right,"* he says: "meaning, those who have these characteristics are the companions of the Right Hand."

*These characteristics* — the ones the passage has just been listing. The verdict is not pronounced on a name or a lineage but on a described life: the deeds, the faith in the heart that sought Allah's reward, and the mutual counsel to patience and to mercy. Whoever has those, says Ibn Kathir, is of the companions of the Right Hand.

## Living it

Taking the passage exactly as the sources present it:

**Check the heart under the deed.** Ibn Kathir's phrase is the standard: "a believer in his heart, seeking the reward of that from Allah." The two ayat he cites make the same point from the other side — the striving is appreciated *while he is believer*.

**Do not climb alone.** *Tawāṣaw* is mutual. Good actions by themselves, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading, are "not enough for raising the all round stature of the Muslim community." Teaching virtue to others is described as an obligation — and mutuality means also being willing to be taught.

**Counsel the two things this ayah names.** Steadiness — which by the definition given here means both withholding oneself from evil deeds and acting upon good ones — and mercy. Encourage someone in *ṣabr* when obedience is costing them; encourage them in *marḥamah* when they have been given a reason to be hard.

**Be patient with people, and merciful to the same people.** That is Ibn Kathir's pairing: patience "with the harms of the people," and mercy "with them." The passage does not offer the option of enduring people without also being merciful to them.

**Extend mercy where it is easiest to neglect.** The hadith Ibn Kathir cites from Abu Dawud names the children and the elders. And the mercy defined by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān includes the restraining half: abstain from hurting people.

**Remember the exchange.** Be merciful to those who are on the earth, and He Who is above the heavens will be merciful to you. That is the promise the sources place at the heart of this ayah — and those who live this way are the ones ayah 18 calls the people of the right.

passages.title: The deniers: people of the left, sealed Fire
passages.tafsir:
## What these two ayat are doing

These are the last two ayat of Sūrah al-Balad, and together they form one half of a verdict. In ayah 18 Allah has just named those who climbed the steep path and called them **aṣḥāb al-maymanah** — as Ibn Kathir explains, *"those who have these characteristics are the companions of the Right Hand."* Ayah 19 turns to face the opposite party, and ayah 20 tells you where they end up. The two ayat are inseparable: ayah 19 identifies the people, ayah 20 shows the door closing behind them.

Ibn Kathir gives this closing section its own heading: *"The Companions of the Left Hand and Their Recompense."* That is the shape — first who they are, then what awaits them.

---

## Ayah 19: "those who disbelieved in Our signs"

**وَٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ بِـَٔايَٰتِنَا هُمْ أَصْحَٰبُ ٱلْمَشْـَٔمَةِ**
*"But those who disbelieved in Our Ayat, they are those on the Left."*

Ibn Kathir's gloss on **aṣḥāb al-mashʾamah** is short and exact: *"meaning, the companions of the Left Hand."* The phrase is built as the mirror image of **aṣḥāb al-maymanah** in ayah 18 — the companions of the Right Hand. The sūrah ends by sorting humanity into two groups standing on two sides, and it does so with two matched titles so that the reader cannot miss that this is one judgement with two outcomes.

**What are "Our Ayat" that they denied?** *Āyāt* means signs — and the sūrah has been laying them out from the beginning. Allah has already asked, in ayat 8–10:

> *"Have We not made for him two eyes? And a tongue and two lips? And shown him the two ways?"*

Ibn Kathir explains each: the two eyes are *"for him to see with them"*; the tongue is *"for him to speak with, and so that he can express that which is inside of him"*; the two lips help *"with speaking, eating food, and beautifying his face and his mouth."* And the two ways — Ibn Kathir titles that section *"The Ability to distinguish between Good and Evil is also a Blessing."* He reports from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd that "the two ways" means *"the good and the evil,"* and says the like is reported from ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Abū Wāʾil, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, and ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī among others. He then cites the parallel from Sūrat al-Insān: *"Verily, We showed him the way, whether he be grateful or ungrateful"* (76:3).

So the equipment was issued and the road was signposted. Eyes to see, a tongue to speak, a clear knowledge of good and evil. The one described in ayah 19 had all of that and still refused. That is what makes this a verdict and not a misfortune.

**And notice what these people are contrasted with.** They are not set against people who merely held a correct opinion. They are set against people who *did* something — and who then, as Ibn Kathir puts it, *"along with these beautiful and pure characteristics, he was a believer in his heart, seeking the reward of that from Allah."* Ayah 18's party is also known for what it urged on others. Ibn Kathir reads their description as believers *"who worked righteous deeds, and advised each other to be patient with the harms of the people, and to be merciful with them."* Maʿārif ul Qurʾān adds that this mutual urging is a **socio-moral obligation** — the believer *"ought to teach his other Muslim brothers to be patient and to be merciful"* — and defines the two words: **ṣabr** (patience) is *"to withhold oneself from evil deeds and to act upon good deeds,"* and **marḥamah** (mercy) is *"to show mercy to one another or to empathise with others and abstain from hurting them."* Of these two together it says: *"This embraces almost all the injunctions of the entire religion."*

Ayah 19, then, is the shadow cast by that whole portrait. The people of the Left stood outside all of it: outside faith, outside the deeds, outside the mutual urging to patience and mercy.

---

## Ayah 20: the word *muʾṣadah*

**عَلَيْهِمْ نَارٌ مُّؤْصَدَةٌ**
*"Upon them Fire will be Muʾṣadah"* — the Fire will be sealed over them.

The Arabic is three words: *upon them — a Fire — sealed*. Everything hangs on that last word, and the early authorities are unusually unanimous about it. Ibn Kathir explains: *"meaning, it will be sealed over them and there will be no way for them to avoid it, nor will they have any way out."* He then lists Abū Hurayrah, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Mujāhid, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī, ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and as-Suddī, all of whom said of *muʾṣadah*: **"This means shut."**

Then three of them press the image further, each closing off one more possibility:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās:** *"Its doors will be closed."*
- **Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk:** *"It will be sealed over them and it will have no door."*
- **Qatādah:** *"It will be shut and there will be no light in it, no crevice, and no way out of it forever."*

Read them in that order and you watch hope being taken away by degrees. First the doors are shut — but a shut door is still a door. Then aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk removes the door itself: there is nothing there to be opened. Then Qatādah removes even a crack of light — no crevice, and no way out *forever*. What these commentators dwell on is not the heat, the flames or the torment; every one of them dwells on the **closing**. What the ayah presses on you is not primarily pain but enclosure: sealed in, with nothing to work on, nothing to pry at, nothing to wait for.

That is the shattering contrast with the sūrah's central image. In ayah 11 the human being is reproached because *"he has not attempted to pass on the path that is steep."* Ibn Zayd read that as *"will he not traverse upon the path which contains salvation and good?"* A steep path is hard, but a steep path is an **opening** — it goes somewhere. The Fire of ayah 20 is the exact opposite: a place with no path out at all. The one who would not climb ends where climbing is no longer possible.

---

## The Fire that others were ransomed from

Ayah 20 speaks of a Fire that closes over people. It is worth setting beside it the aḥādīth Ibn Kathir brings in this same sūrah, because they speak in the very currency of ayah 20: they are about being **freed from the Fire**.

Imām Aḥmad recorded from Saʿīd ibn Marjānah, who heard Abū Hurayrah say that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> *"Whoever frees a believing slave, Allah will free for every limb (of the slave) one of his limbs from the Fire. This is to such an extent that He will free a hand for a hand, a leg for a leg, and a private part for a private part."*

Ibn Kathir notes that al-Bukhārī, Muslim, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʾī all recorded this ḥadīth from Saʿīd ibn Marjānah. And he preserves what happened the moment it was heard. ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn asked Saʿīd, "Did you hear this from Abū Hurayrah?" Saʿīd replied, "Yes." Then, in Ibn Kathir's words, ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn *"said to a slave boy that he owned who was the swiftest of his servants, 'Call Muṭarrif!' So when the slave was brought before him he said, 'Go, for you are free for the Face of Allah.'"* He did not put it off to a better season. He sent his quickest servant, and in that same sitting a man walked out free — freed, in his own words, **for the Face of Allah**.

Imām Aḥmad also recorded from ʿAmr ibn ʿAbasah that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"Whoever builds a Masjid so that Allah may be remembered in it, Allah will build a house for him in Paradise; and whoever frees a Muslim person, then it will be his **ransom from Hell**; and whoever grows grey in Islam, then it will be a light for him on the Day of Judgement."*

Set that word — *ransom* — beside ayah 20. A ransom is what gets a captive out. The people of the Right paid it, limb for limb. Ayah 19 describes those who paid nothing, and ayah 20 shows them with no ransom, no door, and no exit.

---

## Living it

**The surest way not to be described by ayah 19 is to be described by ayah 18.** Allah put the two verdicts side by side on purpose. Ayah 18's people are known by faith that showed itself in action, and by the fact that they would not keep patience and mercy to themselves. Read ayah 19 and ask honestly which of the two descriptions your week would place you in.

**Do it now, as ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn did.** He confirmed the report from the man who had heard it, and acted in the same sitting. Ayah 20 describes the moment when acting is no longer possible; every moment before it is an open door.

**Do not carry it alone.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān's point is that the believer is not finished when his own record is clean — he owes his brothers the teaching of ṣabr and marḥamah. Ayat 18–20 divide people into two *parties*, not two isolated individuals. You climb in company, urging one another on.

**And remember what the seal answers to.** The Fire of ayah 20 has no crevice because the disbelief of ayah 19 admitted no signs — not the eyes, not the tongue, not the two clearly marked roads. The mercy hidden in this closing pair is that Allah told us the ending while the road is still open beneath our feet.

With ayah 20 the sūrah ends. As Ibn Kathir writes at the close: *"This is the end of the Tafsir of Surat Al-Balad, and all praise and blessings are due to Allah."*
